Despite the process's irreversible nature, the final outcome appears to be equivalent to a reversible Ising model with an interacting spin system, based on extensive computational trials.  These trials included both equilibrium and non-equilibrium analyses.

This research proposes a deep learning approach using the Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) to locate and classify sound events. We introduce a new technique employing a 2D filter to extract spatial features from audio data. Furthermore, to mitigate the effect of unbalanced class sizes in the Sound Event Detection and Localization dataset, we present a method involving channel interlacing. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outcomes in a superior mean average precision (MAP) of 51.69% for multiple class sound event recognition.
Concurrent transmission technology has the potential to significantly enhance wireless system capabilities, outperforming traditional transmission methods. This comprehensive review.

This research explores a statistical characterization of the spectrogram's texture, leveraging its second-moment volume to evaluate a signal's uniqueness and similarity to a given reference. To achieve this, a geometric approach is employed that utilizes a randomized, ensemble-based methodology to establish probabilistic bounds on the spectrogram's geometry. This signal evaluation technique is demonstrated to be an effective similarity measure, with a notable advantage over traditional signal evaluation methods like the $l_2$ metric.

In large groups of spiking neurons, whether biological or artificial, it's crucial to identify and analyze different patterns of behavior, such as synchronized groups, loose chimera patterns, and other complex states. To do this, researchers use various methods to detect and characterize these patterns in both small and large networks. However, detecting loose chimera states is particularly challenging due to their fragile nature and the large variations in network parameters. Here, a new and improved detection method is presented that enhances the existing 'Time and Rank' technique, allowing for more accurate detection of all types of network states, including loose chimera patterns. This updated method improves the 'Time and Rank' approach by reducing errors and improving performance in networks with a wide range of parameter variations. In addition, a modified version of this technique is designed for use with larger network structures and is specifically tailored for detection of synchronized groups. This modified method is based on a combination of local and global measurements from the network, focusing on the 'Time and Rank' approach to identify synchronized groups. To verify the effectiveness of these methods, a range of numerical simulations was conducted across various network structures, demonstrating the improved detection of loose chimera patterns and synchronized groups using these modified techniques.

The variant of N-body simulation known as "XREBOUNDr3m" utilizes randomized forces as an anti-interference measure to minimize artifacts resulting from resonance triads, which are identified through the REBOUND's zonal harmonics analyzer. A randomized force with a low coefficient is applied to bodies in a resonance triad to break symmetry and prevent artificial mean motions. This method does not rely on determining the exact resonance frequencies, which can be difficult to calculate accurately. By applying the randomized force only when a resonance triad occurs, as opposed to fixing a frequency for each body, XREBOUNDr3m eliminates the need for trial and error or detailed analytical calculations. This approach is demonstrated in a simulation of a four-planet system where REBOUNDr3m successfully prevents the formation of artificial mean motion resonances.

In many biological systems, regulatory responses aren't just one-way, with outputs influencing further adjustments through feedback loops. This two-way interaction demands a more sophisticated mathematical model, one that surpasses the limitations of traditional Lotka equations. Instead, we turn to quantum mechanics and the Langevin equation to develop a higher-dimensional equation that accurately reflects these feedback dynamics. Although initially surprising, this approach is actually a natural extension of mathematical and computational methods. By simplifying this complex equation, we arrive at a fundamental equation that underpins a wider range of computational methods, all of which are grounded in the same underlying quantum mechanics.

Two-dimensional flow past a barred disc is examined in a situation where a stream of fluid is moving parallel to the disc when the stream's velocity matches the disc's rotational velocity or when the stream's velocity alternates between the disc's rotational velocity in either direction. The scenarios result in a series of blocked areas with curved edges, separating the velocity field into interconnected regions of alternating velocity differences relative to the lab frame, resulting in an infinite sequence of harmonic components. The curvature of boundary lines defining these areas is analyzed, and formulas for their general form are derived based on a specific order of the sequence, along with an investigation of their behavior as the order increases. The spatial arrangement of areas with higher velocities and slower velocities is determined, and it is observed that this arrangement does not depend on the direction of alternating velocities. The effect of a channel's width on the velocity field is also considered.

Analysis of global climate patterns has shown that El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) produces distinct variations in precipitation across different regions of the world. This research focuses on a specific type of ENSO, referred to as a "Unique ENSO," which occurs when there's a unique combination of El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na years within a longer time period. By examining the spatial distribution of precipitation during these years, this study found that areas near the equator experience opposite precipitation trends compared to regions at higher latitudes. This pattern holds true for most parts of the world, with one notable exception: the Amazon rainforest. Further investigation has revealed that Unique ENSO events are associated with a significant decline in rainfall in the north-east of the Amazon basin during non-dry seasons, while their impact on the south-east is relatively minor. To understand the global climate dynamics, this study used a statistical model to identify the underlying climate patterns that contribute to the distribution of precipitation during Unique ENSO years. The results show that these patterns are influenced by both local and remote climate factors, with the ENSO and Pacific Decadal Variability playing a significant role.

We're proposing a new theory that the seeds of massive black holes are formed in a distinct, unique process, especially in smaller galaxies similar to Leo I. Our argument is based on two key points: (1) the lack of core collapse in these galaxies, as supported by extensive observations, suggests against the collapse of a massive rotating protogalactic cloud; (2) an alternative pathway, involving multiple galactic mergers, could to date, hasn't been noticed due to limited data availability in the past. Our model predicts distinct differences in massive black hole formation pathways, leaving behind observable markers, such as core properties and galactic scaling relationships. By analyzing these indicators, like velocity dispersion and stellar mass, we may be able to identify the process of massive black hole seed formation.

We study the magnetic and transport properties of a flat band in a model of a
kagome alloy that has multiple orbitals. Our results show that the flat band in
this system is extremely sensitive to external conditions and easily collapses.
Conversely, this flat band's existence also greatly enhances the system's
sensitivity to external magnetic fields. Specifically, even at very low magnetic
field strengths, the flat band's impact can still cause the system's electrical
resistance to increase at higher temperatures. Moreover, we find that the flat
band's influence can also be seen in the development of long-range, in-plane
magnetic order in the system. Overall, we conclude that the flat band's presence
is essential for understanding the entire range of properties that this kagome alloy
exhibits.

The rapid growth of genomic and transcriptomic data is significantly expanding our understanding of the human genome.  To efficiently explore and understand the relationships between various genomic characteristics and disease traits, researchers must combine their expertise in different areas of genomics and transcriptomics.  Through a collaborative analysis, researchers can synthesize and interpret the results of genome-wide association studies, as well as comparative analysis of genomic data from different species.  By integrating multiple lines of evidence, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying genomic mechanisms and make new discoveries.  In this study, a team of researchers examined the relationship between 18 human characteristics and the genomic information of three species - humans, mice, and chickens - using genome-wide association data and functional genomic information.  The characteristics studied included diseases and physical traits, as well as behaviors and physiological responses.  By applying a method of evidence integration, researchers discovered new associations between genomic regions and disease traits, and were able to identify the most relevant genomic information based on the strength of the associations.  The study provided new insights into the functional genomic regions and transcription factors involved in the characteristics studied, and highlighted the importance of cross-species comparisons and genomic information from multiple cell types in understanding complex disease traits.

This research focuses on identifying the parameters of block configurations that can be accommodated by a group that acts transitively on flags, given a specific residual system. We find the parameters for a specific configuration and determine the possible groups that can accommodate these parameters, ultimately classifying all possible configurations and their corresponding groups.

This study explores the impact of Coulomb interaction on complex many-electron systems, specifically within confined helium-like ions. By examining the electronic density and entropy of these systems in spaces of varying dimensions (3D, 2D, and 1D), we gain insight into how the Coulomb force affects the distribution of electrons. Moreover, our findings reveal that, in lower spatial dimensions, the electronic density exhibits a significant shift towards the confinement center, demonstrating a significant and non-trivial influence of the Coulomb interaction.

A neutron star-neutron star or black hole-black hole system's mass distribution can be used to determine how gravity behaves at high densities, with a extensive binary scenario offering a unique opportunity to make a definitive gravity test. By analyzing a extensive binary's disk properties and using a correct e-folding time, researchers can calculate the tidal deformability and love numbers that are sensitive to the properties of dense matter. Therefore, an extensive binary observation could provide a breakthrough in understanding dense matter, regardless of the results, as it would be the most stringent constraints applied to the properties of dense matter observed through a gravitational wave observation.

In the course of proving a desired conclusion in multiplicative linear logic, often employed in the semantics of proof and computation, certain logical formulas associated with the proof are eliminated during the proof process. This process is referred to as removal. When a formula is removed from a proof, it is no longer required to appear at the beginning of the proof. A specific type of removal, referred to as cut-removal, is particularly significant, as it facilitates the demonstration of the decidability of the contraction-free fragment of multiplicative linear logic by showing that any contraction-free proof can be transformed into a contraction-free proof without cut formulas. This thesis explores an efficient proof transformation method, cut-elimination, for multiplicative linear logic by combining it with a novel technique for dealing with subproofs, allowing for the removal of certain logical formulas from subproofs. This technique is utilized to derive an alternative proof of the decidability of contraction-free multiplicative linear logic.

In the past few decades, various time series analysis techniques have been applied to study the synchronization among different time sequences. This application has been particularly prevalent in finance. Our approach employs cross-recurrence analysis to examine the synchronization of time sequences. The method involves constructing a cross-recurrence plot for each pair of time sequences and using the resulting patterns to determine their similarity. To the best of our knowledge, our study innovatively applies cross-recurrence analysis to the synchronization of multiple time sequences. Additionally, we have developed a new indicator called the similarity index, which measures the similarity among four sequential time values. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed similarity index. Furthermore, we have identified a distinct pattern in the cross-recurrence plots of highly similar time sequences.

We have developed a new approach for modeling how temporary vibrations in a crystal lattice affect the movement of electrons and spin within it. By creating a mathematical framework that accounts for the dynamic characteristics of the electron, we can derive equations for the electron and spin transport that take into account the influence of local vibrations, which is particularly relevant in describing phenomena at very short timescales. Applying our approach to two specific materials, we observed that the temporary distortions in the crystal lattice have a significant impact on the movement of electrons and spin, which cannot be predicted using the established continuum theory. Furthermore, we analyzed how these distortions affect the movement of electrons and spin in the presence of external magnetic fields, which is of crucial importance in understanding spin transport in such conditions.

Boosting sales through promotional activities like discounts and rewards is a key strategy for many businesses. To achieve this, accurately forecasting the click-through rate (CTR) for upcoming promotions is crucial, as it enables companies to allocate budgets effectively across various advertising channels. However, traditional CTR forecasting models often struggle with "black-box issues" when dealing with untested products, relying on incomplete historical data. To overcome this challenge, our proposed framework evaluates the impact of visual materials on CTR using a neural network, and integrates this insight into a multi-layered long short-term memory (LSTM) model for enhanced forecasting accuracy. The framework's performance is demonstrated on a large e-commerce dataset, where results show significant improvements over traditional single-target-based models, particularly when dealing with new products.

Traditionally, business process management systems relied on flowcharts to model processes, but such representations are insufficient for more complex processes, ultimately leading to the development of enterprise architecture frameworks and specific techniques to address business rules and constraints. Within the context of service-oriented modelling, discipline-specific languages have been proposed to address the complexities of business processes. However, current approaches still struggle to effectively model processes that involve multiple instances of a single process, leading to the introduction of a new technique that enhances case-based modeling by incorporating cardinality restrictions. This technique is explained in detail, with a technical report outlining its application, supported by a reference framework for the SOA methodology.

Wildfires disrupting solar energy by delivering the sun's rays to Earth are a significant issue, particularly when their soot clouds combine with moisture in the atmosphere to block sunlight. To address this problem, utility companies operate dispatch management systems to optimize energy production, but these systems require timely forecasts of wildfire aerosol optical depth. By using a physics-based neural network, we can create an accurate prediction of aerosol optical depth, even in areas with limited satellite data coverage. To achieve this, we've integrated multiple satellite sources and developed a novel approach for estimating aerosol optical depth using machine learning. This method allows us to generate precise forecasts of aerosol optical depth, which can take into account varying weather conditions and wildfire trajectories. As a result, we've created a valuable tool for utility companies to rely on, ensuring they have the data they need to operate their dispatch management systems effectively.

For a location tracking system, our research focuses on determining the cost of maintaining user privacy by calculating the difference between hypothetical and actual probability distributions of location data. We initially investigated the fundamental relationship between these distributions, then identified and evaluated specific external conditions, such as an attacker's knowledge of location patterns or sequencing information. To further refine our analysis, we identified the common characteristics of all possible external conditions and determined the general relationship between the hypothetical and actual probability distributions of location data. We then applied this finding to derive a standard measure of privacy for location data, which can be easily extended to accommodate additional attacker knowledge.

Technical factors, like scanner location and data processing methods, can affect the results of functional connectivity research by limiting the precision of estimated connections. Despite these influences, there's a scarcity of empirical research examining how functional connectivity is impacted by intrinsic factors, such as brain regions, at a detailed, region-specific level. To address this, we conducted an extensive investigation involving 360 brain regions by utilizing advanced multivariate imaging analysis on a large dataset of 501 participants. Our study revealed that functional connections between nearby brain regions in resting-state fMRI data are generally strong, but decrease as the distance between regions increases. We also found that functional connections are more precise in frontal regions, particularly in areas associated with attention and executive function, compared to temporal regions. Furthermore, our results showed that functional connections in both children and adults follow a similar pattern of distance-dependent strength and vary by region. We provide a theoretical explanation for these findings, suggesting that the strength of functional connections is influenced by the balance between conductive and active processes, such as neuronal activity and energy consumption, and that regional differences in strength may be linked to distinct computational requirements of different brain regions.

We establish a condition of a lower Ricci curvature bound for directed networks and explore its implications on the heat equation and the Dirichlet problem. This leads to a new inequality for the heat equation with localized initial conditions. Furthermore, we derive a condition for a lower Ricci curvature bound in directed networks, which results in a new notion of a Dirichlet problem with potentially distinct in and out degree measures. This leads to a characterization of the set of Dirichlet boundary conditions that can be applied in the generalized Dirichlet problem, which is shown to be compact and convex.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed languages have gained significant attention, 
but NLP systems for these languages still struggle with NLP tasks due to 
lacking standard pre-trained models and efficient representations.
This paper introduces a new innovative approach to tackle the low-resource 
challenge in code-mixed languages by developing a unique word representation 
that leverages the transition points within a word to capture its language-mixing 
pattern and its position within a sentence.
Experimental results on Wikipedia categorization data reveal that the proposed 
model surpasses current performance benchmarks.

Our calculations of the density of states for H$_{3}$S reveal that the dispersion of states near the Fermi level is governed by a linear relationship with energy, primarily influenced by phonons from 8 eV below the Fermi level. At lower energies, a significant increase in density of states is observed, primarily resulting from the interaction of electrons with molecular orbitals of sulfur, which occurs at approximately 1 eV below the Fermi level in the lowest applicable pressures. This increase significantly influences the superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S, causing its critical temperature to rise with pressure, contrary to a general trend where an increase in phonon frequency typically results in a decrease of this parameter.

Our investigation is rooted in the core of modern genetics, specifically within the body of work established by the influential Ronald Fisher. This study explores one of the most pivotal concepts in genetics, assesses its validity, and demonstrates its practical utility by illustrating how it can be applied in a real-world experiment to determine the most efficient method for selecting the best seeds from a batch of sunflower varieties.

This work presents a novel, efficient, and resilient approach to bipedal motion assisted by propulsion. Building on previous research in locomotion assisted by thrust, which demonstrated improved energy efficiency when moving from a rear to an aerial gait, this study expands the assisted gait cycle to account for external forces. To achieve this, a hybrid control strategy was developed, combining aerial and supported phases, and incorporating a feedback loop to maintain a steady gait cycle. To minimize energy consumption, this cycle was optimized using the Pontryagin's minimum principle. Both traditional and advanced optimization techniques were employed to identify the most energy-efficient gait patterns. Furthermore, simulations were conducted using different optimization methods to demonstrate the robustness and versatility of the assisted gait cycle in various environments.

This paper presents a visual relocalization technique that uses preconstructed 3D surfel maps for accurate placement of a camera's pose. Unlike previous methods which rely on sparse 3D point clouds, our approach utilizes dense visual features for more robust results. By combining a two-stage relocalization framework with map-assisted monocular localization, we achieve superior performance. Our contributions include: (1) a map-based relocalization technique that uses visual features for efficient results; (2) a monocular relocalization approach that surpasses state-of-the-art performance even when data is partially restricted; and (3) in-depth analysis on how visual and geometric factors impact relocalization success.

Mobile devices can contribute to developing machine learning models using their abundant data and processing capabilities, while keeping sensitive information private by relying on client-side model customization and federated learning. However, this approach faces challenges with model coordination and efficiency, particularly when dealing with large datasets and semi-supervised settings. To address these issues, a new framework is proposed that leverages device capabilities and reduces computational complexity, resulting in significant performance improvements and streamlined model customization. Our findings are validated through a detailed analysis and real-world experiments using a combination of simulated and actual device testbed.

Simulating black hole - neutron star collisions, we've explored the behavior of colliding systems with varying electromagnetic field strength, orientation, and with different equations for neutron star density. Our model includes massive neutrino emissions and predicts strong magnetic fields arise within milliseconds. Before the collision, an intense magnetic field wraps around both objects, merging and strengthening as they collide and merge. Their spatial distribution changes based on the collision angle and magnetic field strength, with more material accumulating in the equatorial plane at higher collision energies. When the collision occurs directly in the plane of the magnetic field, a massive amount of matter and energy is concentrated, with about half of the initial neutron star's mass converted into electromagnetic and kinetic energy. Different neutron star equations of state change the mass of the merged black hole, with more massive stars resulting in stronger magnetic fields and faster rotation. Our simulations indicate that in highly collisionous systems, the merged black hole will not survive for long, as it will eventually decay due to massive neutrino emissions.

We take a Riemannian manifold (M, g) to be compact and smooth. Our research focuses on developing non-trivial, invariant scalar curvature modifications of the Ricci curvature. This will be done by combining scalar curvature with a specific functional, derived from the Chern-Gauss-Bonnet form, to create a varied, invariant curvature class on M.

In a Bayesian setting with limited data and a high-dimensional parameter space, lattice Gibbs sampling can be used to approximate posterior expectations. This method involves discretizing the parameter space into a grid and performing Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations on this lattice. As the grid points converge to the posterior mode through sufficient exploration, the expected values of the sampled quantities consistently converge to their true Bayesian estimates, which are calculated based on the Q-procedure.

We've devised a strategy for creating powerful, localized fields in the terahertz region using grapheme surface plasmons. By positioning a small hole within a graphene patch, we can achieve teraHz-scale field amplification, reaching even higher levels with multiple hole configurations. The strong, localized electric fields produced can be utilized to capture and attach individual nanoparticles based on their charge states, offering a novel approach to controlled nanoparticle positioning.

In a hectic emergency setting, doctors face the daunting task of deciding how long patients require medical attention, making it a critical decision that impacts both treatment effectiveness and resource allocation. To aid doctors in this process, a new approach utilizes historical data to identify typical reaction curves for treatment duration, providing valuable insights that can be incorporated into medical decision making. By applying a curve-fitting technique, emergency department-specific patterns in treatment duration are identified, and these patterns are then used to estimate probable outcomes for individual patients, facilitating more informed decisions. The proposed method surpasses existing single-patient and global model-based techniques in predicting treatment duration and is versatile, as it can be adapted to accommodate both fixed and extended treatment periods.

A growing area of research, focused on collaboration between robots and other agents, is highly relevant to widespread adoption, given the abundance of robots available and the ease with which they can interact with other agents through shared workspaces. However, successful implementation relies on addressing core challenges, including the development of efficient communication, the handling of data transmission noise, and robust navigation through the robot's local map and potential obstacles. In this context, we explore a multi-agent scenario where robots collaborate with each other on a local area network and share a shared, distributed map to achieve a common goal. To tackle these challenges, we present a distributed algorithm for map updating and shared navigation, and evaluate its performance under realistic conditions, including limited processing power and the likelihood of data transmission errors.

The ALICE experiment has examined the impact of the Chiral Magnetic Effect in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV by investigating a correlation between the collision angle and the charge of particles. Within a specific collision geometry, E and B field influences can be distinguished by their sensitivity to charged particles' signs. This study limits the influence of electromagnetic effects through a method that accounts for the angle between the collision plane and the E field, and by considering the charge ratio of particles. By applying this limitation, the influence of the E field can be restricted. Observing that results under these restrictions remain consistent with those without restrictions, the research provides further evidence that the signal observed in heavy ion collisions is not solely caused by electromagnetic effects. Furthermore, the research presents a new method to correct the influence of E field effects, allowing for a more precise study of the Chiral Magnetic Effect.

Research has shown that online crowd behavior can be influenced by system design, but less is known about how crowdfunding succeeds or fails in terms of achieving its ultimate goal of payment.  Our research aimed to identify the crowd indicators that predict a project's donation and completion rates on the crowdfunding platform Giggler.  We employed a multi-method approach, combining data analysis and surveys to examine the relationships between these indicators and the outcomes we were studying.  From the data, we selected six potential indicators: a project's description, images, videos, updates, comments, and backer lists.  Our findings from the data phase indicated that projects with descriptions, but no videos or images, were more likely to be successful.  However, projects with the most updates and comments actually had lower success rates.  Surveys with project creators provided further insights, revealing that while videos were seen as essential by the project owners, they did not appear to be crucial for the crowd.  In fact, our numerical results showed that projects with videos had lower success rates.  These findings have important implications for the design of crowdfunding systems and how project creators present their projects to the crowd.

Cybersecurity is a pressing issue for organizations of all sizes, as they strive to protect their systems from various types of cyber threats. To effectively detect and respond to these threats, a key strategy is using Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), which serve as specific signs of a security breach. By exchanging and sharing IoCs, organizations can stay ahead of the constantly evolving cyber landscape and enhance their security. However, exchanging IoCs poses significant challenges, including data privacy and confidentiality concerns. To address these issues, a novel approach is presented, which facilitates the secure exchange of IoCs through a decentralized framework. This framework is built around a distributed training method, allowing each organization to contribute to the training of a shared model without revealing its local data. As a result, each organization can tailor the trained model to its specific needs, providing benefits such as customized detection capabilities and data confidentiality.

A cluster analysis method has been successfully applied to improve the ordering of multiple robotic arms and to reduce their operating complexity. By grouping tasks based on spatial and temporal connections, robots can work together more efficiently, with fewer instructions, and their performance is minimized regardless of their configuration. We present various approaches to establish clusters of related tasks and demonstrate that using avaricious clustering, which prioritizes the largest groups, results in the most efficient robot operation compared to other clustering methods. Additionally, we show that using task positions instead of their weights when defining clusters does not significantly affect the overall quality of the solution.

A next-generation electronics platform known as high agility FETs (HiA FETs), which go beyond conventional MOSFETs, are required for sophisticated quantum electronics and other cutting-edge devices that rely on quantum mechanics. Conventional MOSFETs are inadequate as quantum interfaces due to their slow dynamics compared to quantum processes. HiA FETs, on the other hand, are designed to operate at speeds comparable to those of electrons. We have successfully manufactured HiA FETs using a standard 300mm CMOS process with a gate length of 20nm, achieving a switching time of 1DS. The gates are uniquely designed with a flower-shaped pattern that minimizes electrical charge, allowing the device to switch more quickly. The use of standard equipment and components is a significant advantage of this manufacturing process, as it enables the production of large quantities of devices with identical properties.

This study examines the synchronization of coupled neural teams, specifically how their internal properties affect synchronization, given variations in system parameters between teams. By applying the Lyapunov method and Lyapunov function, we demonstrate that the coupled neural system is stable under a certain condition and show that synchronization occurs uniformly across all teams under a specified feedback mechanism. The study further explores how the structure of team connections influences synchronization and stability, highlighting the importance of team internal connections on overall performance.

To ensure fairness in media and communication, governments regulate the sale of video games to minors with age rating systems. But can these ratings accurately reflect the diversity of content within different platforms? To investigate this question, we created a virtual user to test the age ratings of Netflix, a platform that has no explicit age restrictions but uses source variability to limit access to certain content based on users' profiles. By analyzing the content shown to a virtual user of different ages on Netflix, we discovered significant variations in source variability, indicating that the platform's content is not evenly distributed across all age groups.

In a supersymmetric effective field theory with a Wess-Zumino type coupling, we explore the consequences of introducing a twisted boundary anomaly. This is achieved by representing the twisted PSU(2,2|4) symmetry as a set of composite operators that form a braid group, where we establish that the anomaly arises from a non-singular coefficient in the bootstrap integral of the Wess-Zumino type four-point function. We further demonstrate that the twisted anomaly leads to a shift in the monodromy operator of the conformal field theory, thereby generalizing previous findings of Moncker and Slotin.

We have found an elliptic surface, defined over a cubic Galois field extension of the rationals, at which the rank of the rational points is 13. The surface is defined by a specific construction involving three projective elements from a specific cubic field, and its associated elliptic curve has a rank of 10. This discovery demonstrates that there exists an elliptic surface over a cubic Galois field extension of the rationals, at which the rank of the rational points is greater than or equal to 13.

In crowded wireless environments, a single node's transmission can be disrupted by multiple interfering nodes from opposite directions. For efficient medium access control, it's crucial to consider interference relationships between nodes. However, traditional approaches that rely on acknowledged distances between nodes are insufficient due to unknown distances and moving interferers. To tackle this issue, this study proposes a stochastic medium access control approach, where a transmitting node accounts for variable distances and unpredictable motion of potential interferers from various directions. By assuming that incoming interferers follow a Poisson distribution, the study develops a theoretical model and tests it against real-world data. The results show that this approach closely matches real interference patterns, outperforming traditional methods that solely use signal strength and timeout techniques.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in node classification. However, these models have a major drawback: they require a fully labeled training graph, which is often difficult to obtain in practice. Even a small number of labels can be enough to achieve good results if the labels are distributed efficiently. Our method, pseudo-tagging, involves creating artificial labels for unlabeled nodes by assigning them to the class of their nearest neighbor. This simple approach has several benefits: it's computationally efficient, improves representation, and reduces class imbalances. We've tested pseudo-tagging in conjunction with GNNs on various node classification tasks and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing performance.

In the area of interest point-based action recognition, connecting nearby templates in consecutive video frames is crucial. However, the temporary displacement of these templates necessitates adjustment for accurate alignment, a process typically accomplished through iterative process like SIFT or Feature Matching. This paper introduces PatchNet, a direct template alignment method utilizing learned features and PatchNet itself in a network architecture. Unlike traditional frame-by-frame alignment, our approach considers long-term video structure insights, yielding superior performance with improved efficiency. Our results demonstrate PatchNet's superiority over existing methods on NTU-RGB+D and CMU KINETOCHIC datasets.

We're working with a system called the discrete time asymmetric simple exclusion process on a graph with multiple points where tokens can be added and removed simultaneously. Our findings extend those of [7] to this more complex system. We've developed a method for determining how tokens are distributed in a particular moment, especially when the system is in a state of equilibrium. Our method allows tokens to be added at different speeds at each of several points, and we can also remove tokens at these points with varying rates or not at all. Our main discovery is a formula for calculating the probability of a specific token arrangement at a particular moment, and we've found that, under certain conditions, these probabilities remain constant over time.

A new technique has been proposed to address the growing demand for battery consumption in wireless devices. Wireless power transfer offers a solution by enabling devices to harness energy from their transceivers without needing external power sources. However, achieving simultaneous data transmission and power transfer is challenging due to concurrent interference in both processes. Research has focused on developing efficient schemes, but they were primarily tested under specific system assumptions and did not consider universal solutions. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel approach that allocates resources optimally to support simultaneous wireless power transfer and data communication. By reformulating the non-convex optimization problem using alternative optimization and convex approximation techniques, this framework can be solved efficiently. Additionally, the proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various system configurations, including single- and multi-antenna systems, under different system assumptions. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in maximizing energy transfer while ensuring data rate requirements and maintaining power transfer efficiency.

We examine the behavior of repulsive fermionic mixtures in the SU(N) U(1) sector with general spinor components using the Z2 Gaussian gas approach. By applying a novel gas analogy, where fermions are represented by magnetic monopoles, we derive an accurate analytical formula for the ground state energy. This formula showcases the connections between magnetic monopole properties and fermionic system characteristics. Furthermore, we validate the findings through Monte Carlo simulations.

We derive a classical electrical circuit model for single-tone microwave optomechanics. It involves analzying the nonlinear Hamiltonian of the optomechanical system using a specific transformation. This results in two distinct harmonic oscillators with one of the oscillators representing the mechanical motion. Furthermore, we define a kinetic energy storage coefficient and develop a classical amplifier model describing the optomechanical system's behavior.

In the study of random matrices, universal characteristics are features that appear across all members of a given class, regardless of their specific characteristics. The Airy function, which is associated with the spectrum of three key types of random matrices - Hermitian, unitary, and normal - plays a crucial role in this field. When examining these matrices, the general, non-universal aspects of the associated density of states are often disregarded, and specialists focus on discovering the universal, Airy-based components of the density of states. The current understanding holds that only one universal Airy-based polynomial exists, which is of order three, and is supported by numerous scientific works. This article presents a novel, second-order universal Airy polynomial, derived from the study of three specific, Hermitian matrix ensembles and highlights its advantages through comparison with the existing third-order polynomial.

In this study, we explore the potential benefits and challenges of robots that persistently attach themselves to obstacles, examining how their consistent presence might affect wildlife and ecosystems. To understand the allure of these robots as research tools, we consider their potential impact on marine life in particular, but ultimately find that their presence is unlikely to significantly deviate from regular patterns.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a covariant theory on the 2-dimensional Lorentzian manifold's spacetime, its observables being first-class.

In our research, we examine the impact of smoke reduction on observing images within laparoscopic surgery procedures. To assess the benefit, we created two datasets, one from real surgical videos and the other with smoke artificially added, to test the performance of smoke localization. Focusing on the smoke's visual effect, we developed a smoke detection model using a gradient information-based method, which proved effective in both datasets. To our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize image improvement for identifying smoke in surgical videos and we found that removing smoke can enhance the model's accuracy in detecting the smoke's presence. Conversely, introducing smoke decreased performance. Our research suggests that a smoke-free environment is desirable for optimal object detection in surgical videos.

This research proposes a solution to the frequency-scheduling problem in the Mo\o ller-S\o rensen quantum gate, allowing it to operate with high precision despite the occurrence of frequency errors. By utilizing a trapped-ion implementation that involves multiple modes, our plan involves giving each laser pulse a specific amplitude to compensate for frequency discrepancies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using a simulation that accounts for a wide range of technical complexities, including laser pulse amplitude modulation, the presence of wobbling modes, and a variety of atomic transition frequencies.

By utilizing advanced electron microscopy techniques, researchers have discovered that certain materials, such as BaTiO3 and related compounds, exhibit a paraelectric phase at room temperature, characterized by disordered titanium positions. This contrasts regular images of paraelectric phases, suggesting that the materials' structural stability is influenced by the local arrangement of atoms. To gain a clearer understanding, researchers have created a comprehensive database of possible crystal structures in the (100) plane, based on different atomic configurations, and analyzed the 2D structure of the pseudo-perovskite region, and the resulting images are comparable to experimental findings, highlighting the significance of local atom arrangements in determining the materials' behavior.

Multivariate random fields are widely used to model complex systems in various fields, including weather, genetic data, and brain activity. Stochastic processes offer a broad family of distributions that can be applied to develop the necessary models. The graphical Gaussian process (GGP) is a recent approach that extends the Gaussian graphical model to study dependencies in random fields, but it has limitations in modeling functional data and inter-variable relationships. The functional Gaussian graphical framework is a more general methodological level on which graphical models can be developed. Our study introduces a novel way to interpret GGPs within this framework, enabling the use of advanced methods in functional statistics and optimization to analyze GGP parameters and improve their estimation.

Deterministic methods for constructing repeating patterns in circuits, such as C^n H^n, are commonly used but are computationally inefficient ( exponential time complexity) when generating large sequences of these circuits. A new, efficient (polynomial time complexity) deterministic method is developed to construct these circuits, specifically when the inner gate is a controlled rotation (C_u(theta)). This novel method combines the advantages of both random and deterministic methods, allowing for the generation of both random and structured output states.

We investigate how various forms of regression can be solved efficiently when working with high-dimensional data and uncertain parameters. By using statistical concepts, we develop a classification of these problems into different levels of difficulty. This classification reveals that average-case problems with noisy data can be tackled using stable regression methods, while problems with significant parameter variations require more robust and family-specific techniques. Moreover, we show that even small amounts of data can provide accurate estimates for these problems, surpassing their worst-case counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate that our findings are not isolated to regression tasks, but rather are a part of a broader category of challenging statistical issues.

We've created a polaron model for interaction between light and charge carriers in bilayer semiconductors with indirect gaps, which is also representative of multilayer structures and certain three-dimensional materials like infinite graphene. In these systems, physical properties are mediated by van der Waals forces that cause energy levels to shift and result in vertically stacked quantum wells with electronically bound pairs at the interface, which is equivalent to exciton condensates. Our model demonstrates that these pairs have a tendency to move vertically, which is a characteristic of type-II heterostructures, while also examining the effects of coupling between light and these pairs, and comparing these effects to those of single-particle systems.

In various applications, precise location tracking is essential: for instance, in construction, across platforms such as Android and iOS, and across different radio frequency signals. Since performance depends heavily on available RF signals and is consequently vulnerable to interference, interference-free location tracking is often a challenge. Despite the resilience of many localization algorithms to interference, they were not designed with it in mind and therefore do not adapt to changing environments. If an adaptive algorithm were possible, it's likely that more accurate results could be achieved by reinterpreting and recasting location data in the context of remaining signals, rather than starting over from available data. Although this idea has been explored in other contexts, research into signal-based location tracking is scarce. In our study, we develop and test an innovative technique that re-evaluates and re-interpret RF signal data to determine whether adaptive localization is feasible. Our results indicate that by selectively transferring information between signals, we can enhance the accuracy of location tracking under a variety of conditions.

The $W^\pm Z$ particle pair production in 13 TeV $pp$ interactions is studied using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), where the $W^\pm Z$ signal is identified through their on-shell decays into electrons, muons, and neutrinos. By examining the transverse momentum distribution of the charged-lepton candidate from the $W^\pm Z$ decay, two $W^\pm Z$ signal models are distinguished: the first model represents gauge boson coupled polarization states, while the second model represents the standard model outputs. As a result, the ratio of the first model to the second model is approximately 1.13, where both models are subject to up to three jets in association with the $W^\pm Z$ production.

This paper proposes a new way to understand gravity by utilizing the Cotton tensor, a low-order differential-form manifestation of Einstein's theory. We begin by reviewing the Cotton tensor's definition and its relationship to the Einstein equations. We then provide multiple geometric interpretations of this tensor, which reveal its connection to the Weyl tensor and the Riemann tensor. Furthermore, we establish that the Cotton tensor's divergence is directly related to the energy-momentum source, and its integral significance can be likened to a volume calculation in a three-dimensional space. To illustrate its impact, we modify our conceptual framework to study dust-like particles influenced by gravity, resulting in a simplified analysis of the particles' overall energy-momentum contribution within a closed gravitational system.

The concept of geometric duality is applied to a specific category of orthocomplemented lattices, resulting in the construction of geometric representations for these algebras using polars and spheres within a certain ordered set. Additionally, we examine the relationship between geometric and dual geometric representations for orthocomplemented lattices, demonstrating that they are equivalent.

We introduce a visualization tool called coq-psv that visualizes the progression of a proof in the Coq theorem prover, focusing exclusively on proof steps and their underlying connections. coq-psv allows users to customize visualizations through a web-based interface, providing options to fine-tune the appearance and structure of the visualization. Built with React and D3, coq-psv is fully browser-based, making it accessible without requiring users to download anything. coq-psv can be accessed at coq-psv.io.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of Hecke cusp forms is bounded below by $exp([log(ODE)]^{2})$, where $ODE$ is a specific positive constant, despite the lack of a rigorous computation for $L(1, h\times h)$ for any Hecke cusp form $h$.

When solving equations of the form $Ax = b$, an interior point method uses multiple right-hand sides with varying parameters to locate an optimal solution. Given that each right-hand side is derived from an elliptic PDE, we leverage its smooth nature to develop an early sign of convergence cessation in the Krylov method. Specifically, we use an interior estimate of the residual's gradient to determine when the solution change is negligible, and this approach doesn't require storing historical residual data as in recursive short-recursion algorithms.

We have revisited the terms of large-momentum corrections to heavy-flavor production, specifically the spin-dependent ones, and our work has led to a detailed calculation of a crucial matrix component, known as $A_{gq}^{(3)}$, in the context of polarized deep-inelastic scattering. This new finding enables us to enhance the accuracy of a technique called Variable Flavor Counting, which is used to model such processes. Including our results, we can achieve a 2-loop accuracy in the relevant cross sections and sum over multiple flavor contributions. Our work has also allowed us to derive an accurate value for another important parameter, $C_3^{(3)}$, which will likely have further applications in the study of high-energy processes.

This paper proposes the creation of an AI Incident Repository to document past crises and prevent similar occurrences in the future. Despite significant advancements in AI, its applications continue to be marred by errors, as evident from various ongoing and unresolved issues. To mitigate these mistakes, we suggest establishing an open-source database of AI incidents, similar to aircraft accident reports, which would facilitate learning from past errors and promote the development of more reliable AI technologies.

The renormalization group can be seen as tracing back the effects of systems' size on their properties. A novel numerical approach based on the renormalization group is presented, one that precisely analyzes these size-related influences without relying on scaling assumptions. This method is thoroughly detailed and successfully tested on two simple systems: the Ising model and Kondo model. The Ising model calculations accurately verify the critical exponent predictions made by Wilson, whereas the method allows for solving the exactly soluble curve of the Kondo model across all critical points and temperatures.

Expectations of business-to-consumer online dispute resolution (BCODOR) services lie in effectively resolving consumer complaints through automated decision-making processes. However, current formal expectations for these services, which aim to ensure fairness and lawfulness, are problematic due to the interdependence of these criteria, making it difficult to achieve both simultaneously. To address this issue, we propose using a dual specification method that combines fairness and lawfulness requirements in online dispute resolution contexts. To monitor the compliance of a system with these expectations, the dual specification method is linked to a dispute management system that can identify non-compliant situations and facilitate human intervention in resolving disputes. We demonstrate the practical application of this approach through a case study of the UK's Alternative Dispute Resolution service.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, is designed to efficiently design and execute quantum circuits. Despite its practical benefits, the existing sublanguages used in quantum circuit design lack a comprehensive theoretical framework. To address this, we have developed a formal semantics for Proto-Quipper-M, a sublanguage of Quipper, to provide a clear understanding of its execution. Based on a small-step operational semantics, we have derived a continuous operational semantics, and subsequently, a denotational semantics. By establishing multiple semantics for Proto-Quipper-M, we have paved the way for further enhancements and refinements to this language.

The concept of an outlier in a random matrix is defined as an exceptionally distant eigenvalue from the expected distribution, becoming more pronounced as the matrix size increases. In this study, researchers initially investigated the global statistical behavior of outliers in three stochastic matrix ensembles: the Bertrand-Ramanathan ensemble and two variants of the stochastic block model. Their analysis revealed a distribution of outliers with heavy tails, characterized by a power law, with the same scaling exponent as the Pareto distribution. This was confirmed through multiple approaches, including a finite-size correction argument and a comparison with known distributions. The study further explored the resulting criticality, identifying the point at which the distribution shifts from a power law to a Gaussian, and showing that this transition is linked to the matrix dimension. The study's findings have potential applications in data analysis and can help answer questions previously addressed in statistical physics, such as determining the optimal number of clusters and identifying outliers in data.

We introduce a novel technique for optical phase measurement in a micro-solid state system, utilizing a two-level atom coupled to a cavity and a pair of atomic dipoolar modes. By leveraging a sequence of controlled drives and atomic relaxation, we trigger the generation of duo photons, a state characterized by distinct photon number correlations. To evaluate the system's capability for optical phase sensing, we apply the trio criterion. Moreover, we explore the impact of atomic relaxation and cavity loss on our scheme. Notably, we demonstrate that a low level of red noise can be achieved even with relatively high cavity loss, provided the atom-cavity coupling is strong enough.

Assembling genomes from raw read data is a computationally demanding step in genomics.
A novel, de novo assembly approach using single-molecule, long-range reads has been proposed,
along with a parallel creation algorithm, PCA-Creation. This method takes into account
the reads' implicit geographical relationships within the genome. By employing a graph
data structure and a geographic index, PCA-Creation efficiently and simultaneously
handles all spans among the read pairs by evenly dividing them among multiple processes.
This approach not only eliminates index computation but also prevents process fragmentation.
Furthermore, PCA-Creation's use of contiguous creation ensures that the assembly is free
from spurious, locally-generated overlaps, resulting in high-quality genome assemblies.
Through extensive testing on single-node and cluster configurations, PCA-Creation's performance
has been shown to significantly outperform existing assembly methods.

A novel logistic equation with delayed verification, known as the $\alpha$-logistic equation with a time delay, is studied and it incorporates elements from cellular biology as well as the Malthusian growth model, exhibiting an $S$-shaped pattern, similar to the typical logistic growth curve, but with a longer period of time. The equation exhibits an $S$-shaped pattern in a delayed environment. The global solution's boundedness for any initial condition in a finite population is explored, and its asymptotic behavior is also examined. The solution is demonstrated to converge to a stable equilibrium, either a finite population or a zero population, depending on the value of $\alpha$ and the time delay. The influence of $\alpha$ and the time delay on the solution's behavior is also studied through numerical examples and the solution's convergence to a stable equilibrium is verified.

Many statistical models rely on maximum likelihood estimation, yet this method can struggle when likelihood functions are complex or have unusual shapes. Alternative estimation techniques, such as the median unbiased estimator, are available but only work effectively for linear models. We propose a new approach that allows any estimator to be effective across a wide range of situations. To achieve this, we develop a new measure of an estimator's accuracy and show that, when using this measure, traditional estimators like the mean and median perform well in known situations and provide reliable results in unknown cases. We also provide a method for determining the best estimator in simplified scenarios and demonstrate that, when working within a specific statistical framework, our approach leads to estimators that are similar to those proposed by Bayesians. The method is then illustrated through a case study involving a model with a power-law tail.

A classical electronic circuit or an quantum electronic circuit can coexist as a hybrid circuit. Hybrid circuits leverage the advantages of superconducting technology for high sensitivity and high speed, while also accommodating normal-state components that enable functionality with various inputs or outputs, such as image processing, data transmission, and computation. In this study, we explore an all-in-one hybrid integrated circuit that integrates classical and quantum signal processing capabilities. This circuit integrates an analog classical circuit and a quantum circuit that generates entangled states through the combination of a quantum flux parametric amplifier and additional Josephson junctions. Through numerical simulations, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of this hybrid circuit as a balanced analyzer for detecting both classical and quantum signals.

Measurements of the atomic moments of naturally occurring germanium isotopes have been conducted. The experiments took place at the LANSCE neutron beam facility using a pulsed-field nuclear resonance technique, and the results were obtained at a temperature of 50 mK within a solid-state orientation scaffold. The results for the 60 Ge isotope revealed a nuclear spin of 9/2, which corroborates existing data from both experimental and theoretical sources. The results for the combined atomic moments of the naturally occurring germanium isotopes, particularly focusing on 70 Ge, showed a nearly zero total magnetization, confirming previous experimental findings and expectations from theoretical germanium sample data. The results for the 70 Ge isotope specifically determined a total atomic moment of -0.38(2) Nb, which aligns with theoretical predictions. The results for the 70 Ge isotope demonstrated a significant moment deviation from isotopic averages, which highlights the substantial impact of shell effects in germanium isotopes.

A novel technique for accurately measuring atomic masses quickly, called Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry (Bρ-IMS), is introduced. This method is based on the principle of isochronous mass spectrometry but incorporates a time-varying electric field that is controlled electronically. The space charge of the ion beam is taken into account in the Bρ-IMS method, making it particularly useful for detecting and measuring the masses of short-lived nuclei with high precision. The theoretical foundation and experimental implementation of the Bρ-IMS method are discussed, along with demonstrations of its capabilities for performing high-precision mass measurements of nuclei with very small mass differences.

Multi-level Monte Carlo methods rely on multiple numerical schemes to model lattice field theories. A novel approach seeks to apply neural network-based methods as additional schemes in such models, with these networks often referred to as 'quasi-schemes'. A key requirement is for these networks to be accurate within the statistical uncertainties typically found in lattice field theory simulations. This tutorial outlines the key'standardization' conditions necessary for these networks to meet this requirement, and includes a range of lattice gauge theory examples which demonstrate their implementation.

Enhancing the accuracy of structured text identification (SD) is the key focus of this study. To achieve this, we've developed a novel, external knowledge-based approach that incorporates a specialized preference for regular expressions. By leveraging this technique, along with external knowledge, we've created a more effective indicator for SD. Furthermore, our proposed strategy, guided by this indicator, dramatically improves the confidence of structured text identification. According to our investigation, when applied to various datasets, the top-performing models using both external and internal knowledge showed significantly higher MACE scores compared to individual models relying solely on internal knowledge.

We examine the detection of the top quark and its anti-particle (t-bar) when they collide with nuclei or happen to be produced within them, which might occur in heavy ion collisions at high energies. Participating nuclei can produce quarks, which in turn can generate top quarks through a process called quark gluon plasma. However, detecting these events is complicated because the presence of quarks and gluons in the nucleus makes it difficult to distinguish signals from background noise. To identify t-bar production, we look for signature events that include a large proton, a negative antiparticle, and two heavy quarks, which are indicative of the top quark decaying into a quark and a virtual particle before finally becoming observable as heavy particles. To determine whether detected events represent t-bar production or simply background activity, we compare their characteristics to those predicted by the Standard Model of particle interactions, which includes statistical analysis and comparisons of event patterns. To quantify our understanding of t-bar production in nucleus-nucleus collisions, we calculate a ratio of detected signals to predicted probabilities and compare it to similar values from proton-nucleon collisions, which serves as a benchmark for evaluating our ability to detect t-bar production in nucleus-nucleus collisions.

We tackle the challenging task of parsing natural language to meaningful SQL, spanning multiple domains in a comprehensive manner. Unlike existing research that focuses on a single domain, we aim to make progress on this comprehensive task through an end-to-end, cross-domain approach. To achieve this, we establish a baseline by adapting a successful single-task model from the database literature, and then address two key issues: (a) limited data, a prevalent problem in SQL task, by incorporating pre-trained models, and (b) ambiguous language, by introducing a novel task to identify relevant tables and columns from the natural language input. This supportive task enables the model to learn the necessary patterns and relationships between these query components, which in turn facilitates the model's ability to handle language ambiguities. As a result, our enhanced model demonstrates improved performance on both single-domain and multi-domain datasets, and particularly achieves remarkable gains on the complex restaurant dataset with significant reductions in error rate from 19.6% to 4.2%. Moreover, when applied to the dataset 'ok-cooking', the model achieves an impressive 67.8% error-free rate.

The LoTSS, a large survey covering 355 square degrees at 150 MHz with high sensitivity, has provided valuable insights into the characteristics of radio-bright galaxies and their relationship with their fainter counterparts. By analyzing these sources, researchers gain a deeper understanding of the galaxy evolution process and the mechanisms driving galaxy biasing. Initial data reveal that for every decade in frequency increases, the slope of the galaxy luminosity function shifts by nearly 3 times more than for AGN. To investigate the process of biasing, scientists employed a complex statistical framework and found that, in the LoTSS frequency band, there's no significant difference in biasing between spiral and elliptical galaxies. They also discovered that, on average, galaxies with higher stellar masses experience stronger biasing than those with higher star formation rates. Furthermore, researchers found that the distribution of stellar-to-stellar mass ratio in galaxies shows a distinct variation with radio luminosity, suggesting that more radio-loud galaxies have lower mass-to-light ratios.

The Rank Lasso regression model is an extension of traditional Lasso, allowing multiple features to enter the model simultaneously while penalizing non-essential variables. This property makes Rank Lasso suitable for handling large datasets. Although the Rank Lasso algorithm can efficiently handle a moderate number of variables, it struggles with very large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we present a new adaptive method that significantly improves the scalability of Rank Lasso, enabling it to accurately handle large datasets with a large number of variables. This method is further analyzed, and simulations demonstrate its superior performance, especially when compared to the l1-fused lasso method.

We examine a thermodynamic system undergoing changes in its energy, which lead to the generation of entropy. Our analysis reveals that this entropy generation can be calculated using a localized, convex function of the system's distance from its equilibrium state, which is consistent across various driving mechanisms. This characterization enables the calculation of entropy generation during rapid, gentle changes in the system's control parameter, which is particularly useful in experiments. Additionally, we demonstrate that the conventional time-integration method for calculating entropy generation is invalid under abrupt driving conditions but becomes accurate in cases of slow drivings.

Several environmental issues that were previously neglected are now being addressed due to the increasing awareness of their impact, such as the growing amount of electronic waste. Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions have emerged as a means to mitigate some of these problems, but the environmental benefits of AI-powered solutions, if any exist, are largely unknown. To this end, we aim to uncover the previously overlooked environmental benefits of adopting AI-powered solutions for addressing specific ecological challenges. By taking the example of sustainable transportation, we identify two critical problems - forecasting demand and optimizing routes - and explore how AI can address these issues, only to discover that doing so hides significant environmental consequences. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the primary challenge lies in measuring the extent to which traditional problem-solving approaches like those for demand forecasting and route optimization are actually tackling environmental problems, a hurdle that AI-powered solutions struggle to overcome.

Prescriptive process monitoring, a relatively underdeveloped area of business process management, involves identifying and addressing deviations during process execution to prevent issues at a later stage.  Our approach, which effectively tackles a pressing issue in business processes, involves classifying and interpreting executive decisions made in the course of a business process.  To achieve this, we develop a classification framework that relies on decision theory and similarity measures, and use this to model and identify similar executive decisions, allowing us to prescribe future process courses.  To demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, we conduct extensive analysis on a real-world business process.

This work builds on our previous research where we developed an efficient model for efficiently cooling solid objects and we are expanding on that research to apply the same principles to heated solids. We are working within a simplified framework where the temperature's impact on fluid density is the primary factor, using the Boussinesq model. We are taking a goal-oriented approach, using the Dual Weighted Residual method to minimize goal function errors and adapt the model's parameters to better match experimental data. We are focusing on a specific goal function that takes both spatial and temporal errors into account and our approach is yielding significant error reductions, often by more than an order of magnitude.

A 2019 study by Bodlaender et al. demonstrated that for any fixed stacking height h, multi-level combinatorial optimization problems with restricted height values have simplified, more efficient versions. This work builds upon that finding, revealing that problems with stacking heights between A and B can be broken down into more manageable cases with heights between h and g, for specified values of g and h. To achieve this, we establish a new type of kernelization for such problems, providing evidence that multiple optimization problems with stacking heights are either solvable in polynomial time or have more efficient kernelizations.

In a scenario with interconnected decision-making, where multiple agents prioritize and exchange preferences, we examine how their individual assessments impact the overall network. Our model links each agent's shift in preference to a change in view, and we represent the decision-making process as a dynamic equilibrium, akin to a game theory dynamics. We find that, in the face of a preference change, the effect on the view of another connected agent can be negative, zero, or positive, and the sign depends on the relative importance the other agent places on their relationship. Furthermore, an agent's willingness to prioritize their interactions influences how much their view is affected by the preference change of nearby agents. If an agent highly values their relationships, a nearby agent's preference change will likely result in a positive effect on the view, and this effect can be significant. On the other hand, an agent with less interpersonal connection may experience a negative effect on their view due to a nearby agent's preference change.

A level fuzzy black hole is a type of fuzzy two charged object that has no actual edges and is similar to a black hole in many ways. When studying this type of fuzzy black hole, researchers find that the center of the object remains relatively simple and easy to understand, even though the rest of the object becomes very complex and difficult to analyze as it approaches the point where mass is concentrated. This simplification helps a great deal in calculating key properties such as the Asymptotic Level Fuzzy Black Hole. In our research, we focus specifically on an Asymptotic Level Fuzzy Black Hole with equal electric and magnetic charges. Inside this type of object, we find that the metric and the fuzzy two form can be calculated exactly using a straightforward method. As a result, we are able to determine the behavior of mass, angular momentum and charge in more detail. In particular, we confirm that the relationship between mass, angular momentum and charge is consistent with established principles in physics, and that the ratio of magnetic charge to electric charge varies in accordance with certain predictable patterns.

To understand the relationship between DNA and RNA sequences, we developed a simulation pipeline that models transcription and RNA synthesis in a sequence-specific manner. By applying this pipeline to the human genome, we identified regions with significant delays between DNA and H3.3 chromatin modification, indicating a lag in RNA production. The duration of this lag ranged from a few minutes to over an hour and was influenced by the presence of certain DNA features, particularly strong transcription start sites, pausing sites, and G-quadruplex structures. Furthermore, we observed that high levels of this type of feature were associated with slower RNA production and longer lags.

Recent studies on 64Ni have shown that its low-energy structure is complex and diverse, with multiple isospin and spin orientations exhibiting different modes of nuclear excitation. Notably, a region with no spin orientation (null spin) has been identified, posing a challenge to understanding its properties. To better comprehend this region, a study has been conducted using a 0p0d shell model that incorporates the monopole tensor interaction, revealing new excitation modes that align with experimental observations and enhance the coherence between different excitations within the region.

Chiral supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in various dimensions has a unique dual, allowing for the reconstruction of the Lagrangian from the knowledge of the superconformal indices. This property facilitates the identification of non-supersymmetric counterparts, which we will explore in this review. These counterparts are derived from a combination of two methods: the soft supersymmetry limit and the decoupling of seven additional fermions. While the first approach leads to a straightforward duplication of degrees of freedom, the second approach results in significantly different degrees of freedom. We will examine both methods in the context of four-dimensional and three-dimensional chiral gauge theories and assess their potential applications and outcomes.

A linear complementary set of group codes is defined as a collection of group codes with group multiplicative structures, whose encodings intersect only at the zero element. Our work provides a complete classification of linear complementary sets of group codes over a finite principal ideal domain, with a specific focus on the cyclic code domain.

In many applications involving structural uncertainty, exact inference is crucial. Exact inference within factor graphs can be performed efficiently using algorithms like a message passing scheme, but this method may fail for certain scenarios. By representing a function using a binary representation and introducing an efficient algorithm for exact inference, we can overcome these limitations and provide a quicker solution for exact inference in factor graphs. This new approach leads to a faster and more optimized exact inference algorithm for Markov random fields, comparing favorably to the current best methods.

When sleeping, it's essential to place items that may fall and cause injury in a safe zone. This study proposes an innovative solution for identifying at-risk items in a visualization area using a visual signal and a prone condition signal from audio feedback. By applying the prone condition, the system pinpoints the location of an object, and this research presents various training methods for integrating audio and visual data asynchronously. This solution can function without constant visual feedback and provides real-time object position estimation. Experimental outcomes and case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the asynchronous audio-visual fusion. This research is crucial for creating a system that can monitor a sleeping environment and prevent injuries.

A significant factor affecting the flow resistance of complex shapes is shear stress, and understanding the flow topology around such shapes is crucial for optimizing their design.
